Medical expense tax credit 2026: the CAD 2,890 threshold, which spouse should claim and the 12-month window

A worked guide to the 2026 federal medical expense tax credit: the lesser-of-3%-or-CAD-2,890 threshold, why the lower-income spouse usually claims and when that advice fails, choosing the 12-month period, separate claims for adult dependants, the refundable medical expense supplement and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 10 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration of the 2026 federal medical expense tax credit (METC) and refundable medical expense supplement (RMES) for hypothetical households. Expenses on line 33099 are reduced by the lesser of 3% of the claimant’s net income and CAD 2,890; line 33199 expenses for another dependant are reduced by the lesser of 3% of that dependant’s net income and CAD 2,890. The total (line 33200) earns a 14% non-refundable federal credit, usable only against federal tax left after the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits, which are calculated from the employment income entered with 2026 payroll parameters (taxable income is taken to equal net income). The supplement is the lesser of CAD 1,534 and 25% of line 33200, reduced by 5% of family net income above CAD 33,960, for a claimant with at least CAD 4,478 of working income. Provincial and territorial credits, the disability supports deduction, other credits (age, pension, tuition, disability, donations), the top-up tax credit and Quebec abatement are left out, and all expenses are assumed to be eligible and receipted.

The central idea

For 2026, eligible medical expenses count only above the lesser of 3% of the claimant’s net income and CAD 2,890; the rest earns a 14% federal credit. A lower-income spouse has a lower threshold, but a non-refundable credit is worth nothing to someone with no federal tax, so check the tax that is left before choosing. Picking a 12-month window that holds two years’ bills applies the threshold once instead of twice.

01

What the credit is and how it is calculated

The medical expense tax credit (METC) is a non-refundable federal credit for eligible medical expenses paid by you or your spouse or common-law partner. It reduces federal tax payable; it cannot create a refund on its own. Every province and territory has its own version with its own rate and threshold.

For the 2026 tax year the federal calculation is:

  1. Add up eligible expenses for you, your spouse and your children born in 2009 or later that were paid in a 12-month period ending in 2026 (line 33099).
  2. Subtract the lesser of 3% of the claimant’s net income (line 23600) and CAD 2,890.
  3. Add the allowable amount for each other dependant (line 33199), worked out the same way but with the dependant’s own net income.
  4. Multiply the total (line 33200) by 14%, the lowest federal rate for 2026.
Federal amounts for the medical expense credit
Amount20252026

Net income above which the fixed threshold appliesCAD 94,466.67CAD 96,333.33
Credit rate (lowest federal rate)14.5%14%
Refundable supplement maximumCAD 1,504CAD 1,534
Supplement minimum working incomeCAD 4,390CAD 4,478
Supplement family-income thresholdCAD 33,294CAD 33,960
Family net income at which the supplement endsCAD 63,374CAD 64,640

The 2026 amounts are CRA’s published figures, indexed by 2.0%. The 14% rate follows the cut in the lowest federal rate from 15% (14.5% for 2025 as a whole). The two “at which” rows are derived: CAD 2,890 ÷ 3% and CAD 33,960 + 1,534 ÷ 5%; the 2025 supplement end point matches the CAD 63,374 limit CRA publishes.

Eligible expenses include, among others, prescription drugs, dental and vision care, many medical devices, travel for treatment not available locally, and premiums paid to a private health services plan, including the employee share of a group plan. An amount that was or will be reimbursed by an insurer or employer plan is not eligible. CRA’s RC4065 guide and the folio list what qualifies.

02

The threshold is personal, and that is why the claimant matters

The threshold is based on the net income of the spouse who claims, not on family income. The CRA page itself notes that it may benefit you if the spouse with the lower net income claims. Either spouse can claim expenses for either of them and for their children, whoever’s name is on the receipt, as long as the same expense is not claimed twice.

Below CAD 96,333.33 of net income the threshold is 3% of income; above it, it is the fixed CAD 2,890. Moving the claim from a spouse earning CAD 70,000 (threshold CAD 2,100) to one earning CAD 26,000 (threshold CAD 780) adds CAD 1,320 of allowable expenses and CAD 184.80 of federal credit.

The model’s default is that couple. Person A has CAD 70,000 of employment income; Person B has CAD 26,000 of net income, CAD 20,000 of it from employment. They paid CAD 4,500 of eligible family expenses and CAD 1,800 for an adult child with CAD 9,000 of net income.

“Federal tax left” is the model’s estimate: tax on net income at the 2026 rates, less 14% of the basic personal amount (CAD 16,452), the Canada employment amount (up to CAD 1,501) and base CPP and EI contributions on the employment income entered. Person B’s CAD 966.59 is enough to absorb CAD 735, so here the usual advice holds.

03

When the lower-income spouse is the wrong claimant

A non-refundable credit only reduces tax that would otherwise be payable. If the lower-income spouse owes little or no federal tax, the lower threshold does not help, and the unused medical credit cannot be transferred to the other spouse or carried forward. (Unclaimed expenses can sometimes be claimed in a later year if they fall in a 12-month window ending in that year, but not ones already claimed.)

Three further cases, each computed by the model (2026 federal)
HouseholdBetter claimantValueOther spouse
A CAD 40,000 employment; B CAD 12,000 net, CAD 6,000 employment; CAD 6,000 expensesA: CAD 672 credit + CAD 298 supplementCAD 970B: CAD 789.60 credit wasted, CAD 508 supplement
A CAD 150,000 employment; B no income; CAD 4,500 expensesA: threshold CAD 2,890CAD 225.40B: CAD 630 credit, all wasted

In the first case Person B’s threshold is lower (CAD 360), but B has no federal tax left after the basic personal amount, so B could only collect the refundable supplement. Person A uses the whole CAD 672 credit and also qualifies for a smaller supplement, because the supplement depends on family net income, which is the same whoever claims. In the second case the spouse with no income cannot use any of the credit. The test is simple: compare the federal value, including the supplement, for each spouse. Tax software does this if you try both.

04

Choosing the 12-month period

You may claim expenses paid in any 12-month period ending in the tax year, as long as they were not claimed before. For someone who died in the year, the period is 24 months and must include the date of death. The period does not have to be the calendar year.

This matters when large bills straddle 31 December. Suppose Person B in the default pays CAD 2,250 for dental work in November 2026 and another CAD 2,250 in April 2027:

  • Calendar years: 2026 claim CAD 2,250 − 780 + 1,530 dependant = CAD 3,000, credit CAD 420; 2027 claim CAD 2,250 − 780 = CAD 1,470, credit CAD 205.80. Total CAD 625.80.
  • One window, May 2026 to April 2027, claimed on the 2027 return: CAD 4,500 − 780 + 1,530 = CAD 5,250, credit CAD 735.

The difference, CAD 109.20, is one threshold (CAD 780) at 14%. The cost is waiting a year to claim the 2026 bills, and the 2026 bills cannot also be claimed in 2026. When one year’s share is below the threshold, splitting can lose its credit entirely; the window chart shows this across splits. The model keeps both years at 2026 incomes and amounts; in practice the 2027 threshold and rate may differ.

05

Other dependants: a separate threshold for each one

Line 33199 is for dependants other than your spouse and minor children: for example an adult child, a grandchild, or a parent, grandparent, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew who depended on you for support (relatives other than children must have lived in Canada at some time in the year). For each one, the expenses are reduced by the lesser of 3% of that dependant’s net income and CAD 2,890, so a dependant with little income has almost no threshold. There is no longer a dollar cap on the amount claimed for a dependant.

In the default, the adult child’s CAD 9,000 of income gives a CAD 270 threshold, so CAD 1,530 of the CAD 1,800 counts. Either spouse can include it, and it is added to the claimant’s line 33200, so it also enlarges the base for the supplement.

06

The refundable medical expense supplement

The supplement (line 45200) is refundable: it is paid even if no tax is owed. For 2026 it is the lesser of CAD 1,534 and 25% of the allowable expenses on line 33200 (plus 25% of any disability supports deduction), reduced by 5% of family net income above CAD 33,960. The claimant must be at least 18 at the end of the year, resident in Canada all year, and have at least CAD 4,478 of employment and self-employment income.

Family net income is the claimant’s plus their spouse’s, so the reduction is the same whichever spouse claims; what changes is the claimant’s allowable amount and whether that claimant meets the working-income minimum. For a single person with CAD 18,000 of net income (CAD 9,000 from work) and CAD 3,000 of expenses, the allowable amount is CAD 2,460, the supplement is CAD 615 and the non-refundable credit is wasted because no federal tax is owed. With no working income, as for many retirees, there would be no supplement either.

07

What the official figures show

CRA’s statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) show 5,828,020 returns with an allowable medical expense amount, out of 31,564,160 returns, for a total of CAD 20.33 billion of allowable expenses (after thresholds). That is about 18.5% of returns and an average of about CAD 3,489 per claiming return.

The claim rate peaks at about 30% of returns in the CAD 30,000–50,000 ranges and falls at higher incomes, where the fixed threshold (CAD 2,759 for 2024) applies and couples tend to claim on the lower-income spouse’s return. These are counts of returns, not households, and the averages are allowable amounts after the threshold, not total spending. The pattern is descriptive and does not show why people do or do not claim.

Finance Canada’s 2026 tax expenditure report puts the federal cost of the credit at about CAD 2.2 billion in 2024 and CAD 2.37 billion in 2026, and the supplement at about CAD 230 million and CAD 245 million. The report labels its columns as estimates and projections; later years are projections.

08

A practical checklist

  • Keep receipts and plan statements. Claim only the part not reimbursed by an insurer or employer plan, and include your own share of private health plan premiums.
  • Try each spouse. Compare the federal value for each, counting the supplement and the tax actually left to absorb the credit; add the provincial credit, which has its own threshold and rate.
  • Pick the window. Look at the last 24 months of receipts and choose the 12-month period ending this year that holds the most unclaimed expenses.
  • Claim dependants separately. An adult child or parent with low income has a small threshold of their own.
  • Remember what does not carry. An unused non-refundable credit is not transferable to the other spouse and does not carry forward, but expenses never claimed can still fall in next year’s window.

09

Limits of the model

The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts. It estimates federal tax with the 2026 brackets, treats net income as taxable income, and allows only the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered (self-employment is treated as employment for these credits). Other credits that would use up tax first, such as the age, pension, disability, tuition and donation credits, are not included, so the tax left may be overstated. It assigns all family and dependant expenses to one claimant, assumes every expense is eligible and unreimbursed, and leaves out provincial and territorial credits, the disability supports deduction, the top-up tax credit and the Quebec abatement. Use tax software or the CRA worksheets for your actual return.
